question: What is the primary goal of community mobilisation in Primary Health Care?

options.A: To force communities to accept government policies without question
options.B: To empower communities to take active control over their health and health needs
options.C: To replace traditional healers with foreign medical personnel
options.D: To reduce the workload of hospital-based physicians exclusively

explanation: Community mobilisation aims to empower communities to actively participate in identifying and addressing their own health needs rather than acting as passive recipients. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h1)

question: What role do nurses predominantly play during community mobilisation efforts?

options.B: Sole financial sponsors of health projects

explanation: Nurses act as change agents, educators, and facilitators bridging the healthcare system and the grassroots population. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h1)

question: Why is fostering local ownership an essential objective of community mobilisation?

options.A: It ensures that the government can stop funding health programs entirely
options.B: It increases the long-term sustainability of health projects after external support ends
options.C: It prevents community members from asking questions
options.D: It shifts all legal liability to local residents

explanation: Local ownership ensures that health programs continue to thrive and remain functional long after external funding or NGO support concludes. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following best describes the benefit of mobilising local resources?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any trained healthcare professionals
options.B: It reduces over-reliance on government or external donors
options.C: It guarantees that no diseases will ever occur again
options.D: It transfers all economic control to foreign organizations

explanation: Mobilising local resources helps communities support their own health initiatives, thereby reducing over-reliance on external funding and government budgets. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h2)

question: What does the principle of participation and inclusion emphasize?

options.A: Only male elders should make healthcare decisions
options.B: Every community member, regardless of status or gender, must have a voice
options.C: Participation should be restricted to educated elites
options.D: Foreign experts should make all final choices

explanation: Inclusion ensures that all demographics, including women and marginalized groups, are represented and heard in health decisions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why is cultural sensitivity considered a fundamental principle in mobilisation?

options.A: It prevents community resistance and ensures interventions fit local lifestyles
options.B: It allows health workers to ignore professional nursing guidelines
options.C: It ensures that local traditions are completely abolished
options.D: It speeds up the process by avoiding community meetings

explanation: Respecting local culture and traditions ensures community acceptance and prevents resistance against new health interventions. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h3)

question: Why are traditional and religious leaders referred to as gatekeepers in community mobilisation?

options.A: They physically lock the doors of health facilities
options.B: They hold immense influence over public opinion and behavioral compliance
options.C: They are responsible for funding all hospital equipment
options.D: They act as clinical doctors in rural areas

explanation: Traditional and religious leaders heavily influence their communities, and their endorsement greatly determines whether residents accept health programs. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is a primary responsibility of youth and women groups during mobilisation?

options.A: Acting as active foot soldiers for peer education and mobilization
options.B: Writing national health policies and budgets
options.C: Performing surgical procedures in primary health centers
options.D: Replacing the role of professional nurses entirely

explanation: Youth and women groups often serve as active messengers who spread health information and encourage their peers to participate in health activities. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is the very first step in the community mobilisation process?

options.B: Entry and rapport building with community leaders
options.D: Punishing residents who fail to attend health talks

explanation: Entry and rapport building establish trust and respect with local leaders before any health assessment or intervention begins. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h5)

question: During which step of the mobilisation process are health priorities and local resources jointly identified?
explanation: Community diagnosis involves investigating and prioritizing health problems alongside identifying available local resources. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h5)

question: What is a common reason why communities may exhibit apathy toward new health programs?

options.A: Past neglected promises by governments or NGOs
options.B: An excess of modern medical supplies
options.C: Strict adherence to international nursing ethics

explanation: Communities often become cynical and apathetic when past promises made by authorities or organizations were left unfulfilled. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h6)

question: How can healthcare workers best combat rumors and misinformation in a community?

options.B: By engaging trusted local influencers to debunk myths and use sensitive communication
options.C: By imposing strict legal fines on anyone who asks questions
options.D: By stopping all health education programs

explanation: Engaging trusted local influencers helps correct misconceptions and build trust through culturally appropriate communication. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary difference between monitoring and evaluation?

options.A: Monitoring is continuous tracking of activities, while evaluation assesses long-term impact periodically
options.B: Monitoring is done only at the end, while evaluation is done daily
options.C: Monitoring only measures finances, while evaluation only measures drug dosages
options.D: Monitoring is done by the community, while evaluation is done solely by foreign donors

explanation: Monitoring is ongoing day-to-day tracking, whereas evaluation is a periodic assessment of overall impact and goals. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h7)

question: Why is participatory evaluation important in community health projects?

options.A: It allows community members to assess successes and failures, fostering shared learning
options.B: It shifts all blame for failure onto the community residents
options.C: It removes the need for any data collection tools
options.D: It guarantees that no future funding will be required

explanation: Participatory evaluation involves community members in reviewing outcomes, which promotes mutual learning and local empowerment. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h7)
